source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 22 (PDF 88-100, printed 85-97); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 22 (Hydroxy Compounds), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 In phenols, the hydroxyl group is attached to:
blocks.explanation: Alcohols have the -OH group on an aliphatic carbon; phenols have it on an aryl carbon (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Alcohols and phenols are hydroxy organic compounds with at least one hydroxyl group attached to an aliphatic or an aryl carbon, respectively.

blocks.prompt: 2 Ethanol is also known as:
blocks.explanation: Ethanol is also called ethyl alcohol or grain alcohol; carbolic acid is phenol (Introduction, 22.5).

book_ref.quote: Almost everyone is aware of ethanol, also known as ethyl alcohol or grain alcohol.

blocks.prompt: 3 Phenol solutions were used from 1867 to clean surgical instruments and wounds. Why were alternatives later found?

options.text: Phenol is a gas at room temperature

blocks.explanation: Phenol has potent antiseptic properties, but it burns healthy tissues, so it was too potent and alternatives were found (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Since phenol burns healthy tissues, it was too potent for this use

blocks.prompt: 4 The functional group of all alcohols is:
blocks.explanation: The hydroxyl group (-OH) is the functional group of all alcohols (22.1).

book_ref.quote: Hydroxyl group (-OH) is the functional group of all alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 5 In the general formula ROH of an alcohol, R is:
blocks.explanation: In an alcohol R is an alkyl group; when -OH is on an aryl carbon the compound is a phenol (22.1, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: In an alcohol, R is an alkyl group.

blocks.prompt: 6 Which familiar substances are included in the alcohol family?
blocks.explanation: The alcohol family also includes cholesterol and the carbohydrates (22.1).

book_ref.quote: The family also includes familiar substances as cholesterol and the carbohydrates.

blocks.prompt: 7 The second member of the homologous series of monohydric alcohols is:
blocks.explanation: Methanol (CH₃OH) and ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) are the first two members (22.1).

book_ref.quote: Methanol (CH₃OH) and ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) are the first two members of the homologous series of monohydric alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 8 Glycerol contains three -OH groups. It is classified as a:
blocks.explanation: Alcohols are classified by the number of -OH groups into monohydric and polyhydric; glycerol, with three, is polyhydric (22.1).

book_ref.quote: Depending on the number of hydroxyl groups attached, alcohols can be classified into monohydric and polyhydric alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 9 The IUPAC name of glycol is:
blocks.explanation: Glycol is 1,2-ethanediol and glycerol is 1,2,3-propanetriol (22.1, Book correction of the misspelt labels).

book_ref.quote: they are 1,2-ethanediol and 1,2,3-propanetriol

blocks.prompt: 10 Alcohols are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary according to the number of:

options.text: hydrogen atoms on the oxygen atom
carbon atoms directly attached to the carbon bearing the -OH group
carbon atoms in the longest chain

blocks.explanation: The type depends on the number of carbon atoms directly attached to the carbon bonded to -OH (22.1).

book_ref.quote: Depending on the number of carbon atoms which are directly attached to the carbon that is bonded with the -OH group

blocks.prompt: 11 The general formula of a secondary alcohol is:
blocks.explanation: Primary R₁CH₂OH, secondary R₂CHOH, tertiary R₃COH (22.1).

book_ref.quote: Its general formula is R₂CHOH.

blocks.prompt: 12 Which general formula represents a tertiary alcohol?
blocks.explanation: In a tertiary (3°) alcohol the -OH is on a tertiary carbon: R₃COH (22.1).

book_ref.quote: Its general formula is R₃COH.

blocks.prompt: 13 Propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, is a:
blocks.explanation: The -OH carbon is attached to two carbon atoms, so it is a secondary carbon: propan-2-ol is a 2° alcohol (22.1).

book_ref.quote: A secondary (2°) alcohol is one in which the OH group is attached to a secondary carbon atom.

blocks.prompt: 14 Which of these is a primary alcohol?
blocks.explanation: In propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, the -OH carbon is attached to one carbon only (R₁CH₂OH), so it is primary (22.1).

book_ref.quote: A primary (1°) alcohol is one in which the OH group is attached a primary carbon atom.

blocks.prompt: 15 In the equilibrium ROH(aq) ⇌ RO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq), the position of equilibrium:
blocks.explanation: Alcohols have a low degree of dissociation, so there are far more ROH molecules than ions; the equilibrium lies to the left (22.2).

book_ref.quote: Alcohols have a low degree of dissociation.

blocks.prompt: 16 Alcohols are weaker acids than water because in solution they have:
blocks.explanation: Alcohols have a lower [H⁺(aq)] in solution compared with water, so they are weaker acids (22.2).

book_ref.quote: As alcohols have a lower [H⁺(aq)] in solution compared to water, alcohols are weaker acids than water.

blocks.prompt: 17 Alkyl groups push electrons into a covalent bond. They are said to have:
blocks.explanation: Electron-donating groups such as alkyl groups have a positive inductive effect (22.2).

book_ref.quote: Electron-donating species push electrons into a covalent bond and are said to have a positive inductive effect.

blocks.prompt: 18 The effect of the alkyl group on the ethoxide ion is that it:

options.text: stabilises it by delocalising the charge
destabilises it by increasing electron density on O

blocks.explanation: The electron-donating alkyl group puts more electron density on O and destabilises the alkoxide ion, which readily accepts H⁺ again (22.2).

book_ref.quote: The alkyl groups destabilize the alkoxide ion, which is formed by removing one proton (H⁺) from the alcohol molecule.

blocks.prompt: 19 Because of extra electron density on its oxygen atom, an alkoxide ion is more likely to:

options.text: accept an H⁺ ion and re-form the alcohol
delocalise its charge into a ring

blocks.explanation: With more electron density on O, the alkoxide ion readily accepts H⁺ and forms the alcohol again (22.2).

book_ref.quote: The alkoxide ion is, therefore, more likely to accept an H⁺ ion and form the alcohol again.

blocks.prompt: 20 The conjugate base of phenol is the:
blocks.explanation: Removing H⁺ from phenol gives the phenoxide ion, its conjugate base, stabilised by delocalisation (22.2).

book_ref.quote: The delocalisation stabilises the phenoxide ion, the conjugate base of phenol.

blocks.prompt: 21 The phenoxide ion is stable because:

options.text: an alkyl group pushes electrons onto oxygen
the ring has no π electrons
a lone pair on oxygen overlaps with the ring's delocalised π system

blocks.explanation: A lone pair of oxygen overlaps with the delocalised π system, spreading the negative charge over the ring (22.2).

book_ref.quote: This is possible as one of the lone pairs on the oxygen atom overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring.

blocks.prompt: 22 Compared with the ethoxide ion, the oxygen atom of the phenoxide ion has:
blocks.explanation: Delocalisation leaves less charge density on oxygen, so H⁺ is not strongly attracted back (22.2).

book_ref.quote: Because of this delocalisation, there is less charge density on the oxygen atom.

blocks.prompt: 23 The correct order of acidity is:
blocks.explanation: The relative acidities are phenol > water > ethanol (22.2).

book_ref.quote: The relative acidities are as follows: phenol > water > ethanol

blocks.prompt: 24 Phenol is more likely to:

options.text: gain a proton and act as a base
lose a proton and act as an acid
neither lose nor gain a proton

blocks.explanation: Since the phenoxide ion is stabilised, phenol tends to lose a proton (acid) rather than gain one (22.2).

book_ref.quote: This means that phenol is more likely to lose a proton (and act as an acid) rather than to gain a proton (and act as a base).

blocks.prompt: 25 The catalyst used when ethene reacts with steam to form ethanol is:
blocks.explanation: Hot steam and an alkene with concentrated phosphoric acid as catalyst give an alcohol (22.3 i).

book_ref.quote: When hot steam is reacted with an alkene, using concentrated phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) as a catalyst, electrophilic addition takes place to form an alcohol.

blocks.prompt: 26 The reaction of an alkene with steam to give an alcohol is a type of:
blocks.explanation: With H₃PO₄ as catalyst, electrophilic addition of steam to the alkene takes place (22.3 i).

book_ref.quote: When hot steam is reacted with an alkene, using concentrated phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) as a catalyst, electrophilic addition takes place to form an alcohol.

blocks.prompt: 27 An alkene treated with cold, dilute KMnO₄ forms a:
blocks.explanation: Cold, dilute KMnO₄ is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises an alkene to a diol (22.3 ii).

book_ref.quote: Alcohols are obtained by the oxidation of alkenes with cold, dilute KMnO₄, a mild oxidising agent.

blocks.prompt: 28 Bromoethane heated with aqueous NaOH gives ethanol by:
blocks.explanation: The halogen is replaced by -OH when heated with aqueous NaOH: nucleophilic substitution (22.3 iii).

book_ref.quote: The halogen atom in halogenoalkanes can be substituted by –OH group when heated with aqueous NaOH in a nucleophilic substitution reaction, giving an alcohol.

blocks.prompt: 29 Propanone is reduced with NaBH₄. The product is:
blocks.explanation: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols; propanone gives propan-2-ol (22.3 iv).

book_ref.quote: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 30 Reduction of ethanal with LiAlH₄ gives:
blocks.explanation: Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols; ethanal gives ethanol (22.3 iv).

book_ref.quote: Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 31 Ethanoic acid is converted into ethanol by:
blocks.explanation: Carboxylic acids are reduced by LiAlH₄ to primary alcohols (22.3 v).

book_ref.quote: Similarly, carboxylic acids are reduced by LiAlH₄ to primary alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 32 Ethyl ethanoate heated with dilute acid is hydrolysed to:
blocks.explanation: Hydrolysis of an ester gives a carboxylic acid and an alcohol: ethyl ethanoate gives ethanoic acid and ethanol (22.3 vi).

book_ref.quote: When an ester is heated with dilute acid or alkali, hydrolysis takes place and a carboxylic acid and alcohol are formed.

blocks.prompt: 33 Which of the following is NOT listed as a starting material for preparing alcohols?
blocks.explanation: Alcohols are prepared from alkenes, halogenoalkanes, carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids and esters (22.3).

book_ref.quote: Alcohols can be prepared from alkenes, halogenoalkanes, carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and esters.

blocks.prompt: 34 The products of complete combustion of ethanol are:
blocks.explanation: Alcohols on ignition undergo complete combustion to carbon dioxide and water (22.4 i).

book_ref.quote: Alcohols when ignited, undergo complete combustion to form carbon dioxide and water.

blocks.prompt: 35 In CH₃CH₂OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O, the number of moles of O₂ needed to burn 0.5 mol of ethanol completely is:
blocks.explanation: 1 mol ethanol needs 3 mol O₂, so 0.5 mol needs 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 mol (22.4 i).

book_ref.quote: Alcohols when ignited, undergo complete combustion to form carbon dioxide and water.

blocks.prompt: 36 ΔH°c of ethanol is −1367 kJ mol⁻¹. The heat released when 2 mol of ethanol burn completely is:
blocks.explanation: Heat = 2 × 1367 = 2734 kJ released (22.4 i).

book_ref.quote: The above reaction is highly exothermic; this is why the alcohol is used as an alternate to petrol in some countries.

blocks.prompt: 37 Alcohol is used as an alternative to petrol in some countries because its combustion is:
blocks.explanation: Combustion of ethanol is highly exothermic (ΔH°c = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹), so it is used as a fuel (22.4 i).

book_ref.quote: The above reaction is highly exothermic; this is why the alcohol is used as an alternate to petrol in some countries.

blocks.prompt: 38 When ethanol reacts with HCl in the presence of ZnCl₂, the product is:
blocks.explanation: CH₃CH₂OH + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl + H₂O (ZnCl₂): the -OH is replaced by Cl (22.4 ii).

book_ref.quote: In the substitution of alcohols, a hydroxy group (-OH) is replaced by another substituent (e.g. halogens) to form a new product (e.g., halogenoalkanes).

blocks.prompt: 39 Substitution of the -OH group of an alcohol by a halogen gives a:
blocks.explanation: In substitution, -OH is replaced by a halogen to form a halogenoalkane (22.4 ii).

book_ref.quote: In the substitution of alcohols, a hydroxy group (-OH) is replaced by another substituent (e.g. halogens) to form a new product (e.g., halogenoalkanes).

blocks.prompt: 40 When sodium reacts with an alcohol, the gas given off is:
blocks.explanation: The O-H bond breaks; hydrogen gas is given off and an alkoxide is formed; bubbles of H₂ show an -OH group (22.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: This reaction can be used as a test for hydroxy (-OH) group.

blocks.prompt: 41 Compared with the reaction of sodium with water, its reaction with ethanol is:
blocks.explanation: The reaction with ethanol is less vigorous than with water (22.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: Though the reaction is less vigorous than sodium reacting with water

blocks.prompt: 42 Sodium is added separately to phenolphthalein in ethanol and in water. What is observed?

options.text: Pink colour forms immediately in ethanol but slowly in water
No pink colour forms in either
Orange solution turns green in both
Pink colour forms slowly in ethanol but immediately in water

blocks.explanation: Pink colour forms slowly with ethanol and immediately with water, showing Na reacts more slowly with ethanol (22.4 iii box).

book_ref.quote: When sodium metal is added to a solution of phenolphthalein and ethanol, pink colour is formed slowly.

blocks.prompt: 43 After sodium reacts with ethanol and the excess ethanol is evaporated, the white crystalline solid left is:
blocks.explanation: A white crystalline solid of sodium alkoxide (here sodium ethoxide) is left (22.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: If the excess ethanol is evaporated off after the reaction, a white crystalline solid of sodium alkoxide is left.

blocks.prompt: 44 Which alcohol reacts least vigorously with sodium?
blocks.explanation: The longer the hydrocarbon chain, the less vigorous the reaction; butan-1-ol has the longest chain here (22.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: The longer the hydrocarbon chain in the alcohol, the less vigorous the reaction becomes.

blocks.prompt: 45 Using 2CH₃CH₂OH + 2Na → 2CH₃CH₂ONa + H₂, the moles of H₂ formed from 0.3 mol of ethanol with excess sodium are:
blocks.explanation: 2 mol ethanol give 1 mol H₂, so 0.3 mol give 0.3 ÷ 2 = 0.15 mol (22.4 iii).

book_ref.quote: If the excess ethanol is evaporated off after the reaction, a white crystalline solid of sodium alkoxide is left.

blocks.prompt: 46 Oxidation of ethanol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ first gives:
blocks.explanation: Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes: CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O (22.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: Primary alcohols can be oxidised to form aldehydes and the secondary alcohols can be oxidised to form only ketones using oxidizing agents.

blocks.prompt: 47 Propan-2-ol on oxidation gives:
blocks.explanation: A secondary alcohol is oxidised only to a ketone: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O (22.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: Primary alcohols can be oxidised to form aldehydes and the secondary alcohols can be oxidised to form only ketones using oxidizing agents.

blocks.prompt: 48 Which alcohol does NOT undergo oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇?
blocks.explanation: Tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary (22.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: Tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation.

blocks.prompt: 49 When a primary alcohol is warmed with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, the colour changes from:
blocks.explanation: Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ ions are reduced to green Cr³⁺ ions (22.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: When alcohols are oxidised the orange dichromate ions (Cr₂O₇²⁻) are reduced to green Cr³⁺ ions.

blocks.prompt: 50 The green colour formed when an alcohol reduces acidified dichromate is due to:
blocks.explanation: Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to green Cr³⁺ (22.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: When alcohols are oxidised the orange dichromate ions (Cr₂O₇²⁻) are reduced to green Cr³⁺ ions.

blocks.prompt: 51 Potassium dichromate(VI) is used in an acidic medium because the acid:

options.text: provides the H⁺ ions needed for the dichromate to be reduced

blocks.explanation: The reduction of dichromate requires H⁺ ions, which the acidic medium provides (22.4 iv, Keep in Mind).

book_ref.quote: This reduction requires hydrogen (H⁺) ions which are provided by the acidic medium.

blocks.prompt: 52 The correct name of K₂Cr₂O₇ is:
blocks.explanation: K₂Cr₂O₇ is potassium dichromate(VI); potassium chromate(VI) is K₂CrO₄ (22.4 iv, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: K₂Cr₂O₇ is potassium dichromate(VI), not potassium chromate(VI) (which is K₂CrO₄)

blocks.prompt: 53 Three tubes of warm acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ contain propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. The solution stays orange in the tube with:
blocks.explanation: Only the primary and secondary alcohols turn it green; the tertiary 2-methylpropan-2-ol shows no colour change (22.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: no colour change is observed with 2-methyl-propan-2-ol, which is a tertiary alcohol

blocks.prompt: 54 Besides acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, which oxidising agent is named for alcohols?
blocks.explanation: The oxidising agents for alcohols include acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and acidified KMnO₄; NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ are reducing agents (22.4 iv).

book_ref.quote: The oxidising agents for alcohols include acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and acidified KMnO₄.

blocks.prompt: 55 In a breathalyser, the current measured comes from:

options.text: electrons absorbed when ethanol is oxidised
the reduction of ethanol to ethane
electrons released when ethanol in the breath is oxidised

blocks.explanation: Oxidation releases electrons; the electrons given up by ethanol make the current, proportional to the alcohol (22.4 iv, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: Oxidation releases electrons; it does not require them.

blocks.prompt: 56 The formula of the manganate(VII) ion is:
blocks.explanation: The manganate(VII) ion is MnO₄⁻ (22.4 iv, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: The manganate(VII) ion is printed 'MnO⁴⁻'; its formula is MnO₄⁻.

blocks.prompt: 57 Dehydration of an alcohol is a type of:
blocks.explanation: Dehydration is an elimination reaction in which a water molecule is removed (22.4 v).

book_ref.quote: Dehydration is the type of the elimination reaction in which a water molecule is removed.

blocks.prompt: 58 Dehydration of ethanol gives:
blocks.explanation: Alcohols are dehydrated to alkenes; ethanol gives ethene and water (22.4 v).

book_ref.quote: Alcohols can also undergo dehydration to form alkenes.

blocks.prompt: 59 Which of these is NOT a dehydrating agent for alcohols?
blocks.explanation: Dehydrating agents include aluminium oxide, conc. sulphuric acid and conc. phosphoric acid; NaBH₄ is a reducing agent (22.4 v, 22.3).

book_ref.quote: Dehydrating agents may be aluminium oxide, conc. sulphuric, acid, conc phosphoric acid, etc.

blocks.prompt: 60 The formula of the simplest phenol is:
blocks.explanation: The simplest phenol is C₆H₅OH (22.5).

book_ref.quote: The chemical formula of the simplest phenol is C₆H₅OH.

blocks.prompt: 61 Phenol is also known as:
blocks.explanation: Phenol is also known as carbolic acid and was used as carbolic soap (22.5).

book_ref.quote: Phenol is also known as carbolic acid and was used as carbolic soap.

blocks.prompt: 62 At room conditions phenol is a:
blocks.explanation: Phenol is a crystalline white solid (22.5).

book_ref.quote: Phenol is a crystalline white solid.

blocks.prompt: 63 Which compound is an example of a phenol?
blocks.explanation: Phenol, 2-naphthol and 1-naphthol are examples of phenols (22.5).

book_ref.quote: Examples of phenols: phenol, 2-naphthol and 1-naphthol

blocks.prompt: 64 Phenol can be prepared from phenylamine by reacting it with:
blocks.explanation: Phenols are produced by the reaction of phenylamine with nitrous acid (22.5).

book_ref.quote: Phenols can be produced by the reaction of phenylamine with nitrous acid (HNO₂).

blocks.prompt: 65 The nitrous acid for the preparation of phenol is made in situ from:

options.text: NaOH and HNO₃ at room temperature

blocks.explanation: HNO₂ is unstable, so it is made from sodium nitrite and dilute HCl, kept below 10°C with ice (22.5, Step 1).

book_ref.quote: Step 1 - The HNO₂ is so unstable that it needs to be prepared in a test-tube by reacting sodium nitrite (NaNO₂) and dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) while keeping the temperature below 10°C using ice.

blocks.prompt: 66 Phenylamine reacts with cold nitrous acid to form:
blocks.explanation: Phenylamine reacts with HNO₂ to form an unstable diazonium salt (22.5, Step 2).

book_ref.quote: Step 2 - Phenylamine is then reacted with the HNO₂ to form an unstable diazonium salt

blocks.prompt: 67 In the last step, the diazonium salt is warmed with water. The products are:
blocks.explanation: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl (22.5, Book correction: warming with water, not NaOH).

book_ref.quote: Phenol is made by warming the diazonium salt solution with water

blocks.prompt: 68 If the diazonium salt were warmed with alkali instead of water, the phenol formed would:

options.text: form phenoxide and couple with diazonium ions to give an azo dye

blocks.explanation: In alkali, phenol forms phenoxide, which couples with remaining diazonium ions to give an azo dye (22.5, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: In alkali the phenol would form phenoxide and couple with the remaining diazonium ions to give an azo dye.

blocks.prompt: 69 Phenols show many types of reactions because:

options.text: only the OH group can react
both the electron-rich ring and the polar OH group can react
the ring has no electrons to react

blocks.explanation: Both the electron-rich benzene ring and the polar OH group take part in reactions (22.6).

book_ref.quote: Phenols can undergo many types of reactions as both the electron-rich benzene ring and the polar OH group can participate in chemical reactions.

blocks.prompt: 70 Phenols are only slightly soluble in water because of:
blocks.explanation: The large non-polar benzene ring makes phenols only slightly soluble in water (22.6.1 i).

book_ref.quote: Phenols are only slightly soluble in water due to the large non-polar benzene ring.

blocks.prompt: 71 Phenol dissolves in aqueous NaOH because it forms:

options.text: a soluble salt, sodium phenoxide, and water

blocks.explanation: Phenol undergoes an acid-base reaction with bases to form a soluble salt and water (22.6.1 i).

book_ref.quote: However, they do dissolve in alkaline solutions and undergo acid-base reactions with bases to form a soluble salt and water.

blocks.prompt: 72 Molten phenol reacts with sodium to give:
blocks.explanation: It is an acid-base reaction: a soluble salt is formed and hydrogen gas is given off (22.6.1 ii).

book_ref.quote: Molten phenols react vigorously with reactive metals such as sodium (Na).

blocks.prompt: 73 In the balanced equation for phenol and sodium, the mole ratio phenol : H₂ is:
blocks.explanation: 2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂, so phenol : H₂ = 2 : 1 (22.6.1 ii, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: it is drawn as 2 phenol + 2Na -> 2 sodium phenoxide + H2

blocks.prompt: 74 Phenol heated with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of a base gives phenyl ethanoate, which is:
blocks.explanation: Phenyl ethanoate, CH₃COOC₆H₅, is an ester (22.6.1 iii, Book correction).

book_ref.quote: The product, phenyl ethanoate (CH₃COOC₆H₅), is an ester, not an ether

blocks.prompt: 75 In the reaction of phenol with an acyl chloride, the base is used to:

options.text: deprotonate phenol to the phenoxide ion, a better nucleophile

blocks.explanation: The base deprotonates phenol to the phenoxide ion, a better nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon (22.6.1 iii).

book_ref.quote: The base is needed to deprotonate the phenol and form a phenoxide ion.

blocks.prompt: 76 In the formation of phenyl ethanoate, the phenoxide ion attacks the:
blocks.explanation: The phenoxide ion is a better nucleophile and attacks the carbonyl carbon (22.6.1 iii).

book_ref.quote: The phenoxide ion is a better nucleophile than the original phenol molecule and will be able to attack the carbonyl carbon.

blocks.prompt: 77 The benzene ring of phenol is activated towards electrophiles because:

options.text: the OH group withdraws electrons from the ring
the ring loses its π electrons
the oxygen lone pair delocalises into the ring, increasing its electron density

blocks.explanation: One lone pair of O overlaps with the π system, increasing electron density, so the ring is activated (22.6.2).

book_ref.quote: The oxygen atom in this hydroxyl group donates electron density into the ring.

blocks.prompt: 78 The -OH group of phenol directs incoming electrophiles to positions:
blocks.explanation: Electrophiles are directed to the 2, 4 and 6 positions (22.6.2).

book_ref.quote: The incoming electrophiles are directed by the hydroxyl group of phenol to the 2, 4, and 6 positions.

blocks.prompt: 79 Phenol with dilute HNO₃ at room temperature gives:
blocks.explanation: Dilute HNO₃ at room temperature gives a mixture of 2- and 4-nitrophenol (22.6.2 i).

book_ref.quote: Phenols can undergo electrophilic substitution reactions when reacted with dilute nitric acid (HNO₃) at room temperature to give a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol.

blocks.prompt: 80 In the nitration of phenol, a hydrogen atom of the ring is replaced by:
blocks.explanation: In nitration a ring hydrogen is substituted by a nitro (-NO₂) group (22.6.2 i).

book_ref.quote: A hydrogen atom in the benzene ring is substituted by a nitro (-NO₂) group.

blocks.prompt: 81 Nitration of benzene, unlike that of phenol, needs:

options.text: a mixture of conc. HNO₃ and conc. H₂SO₄ at 25-60°C

blocks.explanation: Benzene needs concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ refluxed at 25-60°C; phenol reacts with dilute HNO₃ at room temperature (22.6.2 i).

book_ref.quote: The nitration of benzene requires a mixture of concentrated nitric acid (HNO₃) and sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) refluxed with benzene between 25°C and 60°C.

blocks.prompt: 82 When phenol is added to bromine water at room temperature:

options.text: no change is seen without a catalyst
the orange colour disappears and a white precipitate forms

blocks.explanation: Phenol decolourises orange bromine water and gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol (22.6.2 ii).

book_ref.quote: Phenol decolourises the orange bromine solution to form a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

blocks.prompt: 83 The white precipitate formed in the bromination of phenol is:
blocks.explanation: Bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol (22.6.2 ii).

book_ref.quote: Phenol decolourises the orange bromine solution to form a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

blocks.prompt: 84 Bromination of benzene requires:

options.text: pure bromine with anhydrous AlBr₃ catalyst

blocks.explanation: Benzene needs pure bromine and anhydrous AlBr₃; phenol reacts readily with bromine water without a catalyst (22.6.2 ii).

book_ref.quote: Benzene will undergo bromination only when reacted with pure bromine (not a solution) and in the presence of anhydrous aluminium bromide (AlBr₃) catalyst at room temperature.

blocks.prompt: 85 Phenol is nitrated under milder conditions than benzene because phenol is:

options.text: a stronger acid than nitric acid

blocks.explanation: Phenol's ring is activated, so it is more reactive and is nitrated with dilute HNO₃ at room temperature (22.6.2 i).

book_ref.quote: Since phenol is more reactive, nitration can occur under milder conditions by reacting it with dilute nitric acid at room temperature.

blocks.prompt: 86 In 1-naphthol, the -OH group is attached to:
blocks.explanation: 1-naphthol has the hydroxy group at position 1 of naphthalene (22.6.2).

book_ref.quote: 1-naphthol contains a hydroxy group attached to position of 1 of naphthalene.

blocks.prompt: 87 In 1-naphthol, incoming electrophiles are directed to:
blocks.explanation: The -OH of 1-naphthol activates the ring and directs electrophiles to the 2 and/or 4 positions (22.6.2).

book_ref.quote: The electrophiles are directed to the 2 and/or 4 positions.

blocks.prompt: 88 Which statement about bromination is correct?

options.text: Phenol reacts with bromine water without a catalyst
Benzene reacts with bromine water without a catalyst
Phenol does not react with bromine

blocks.explanation: Phenol readily reacts with bromine water in the absence of a catalyst; benzene needs pure Br₂ and AlBr₃ (22.6.2 ii).

book_ref.quote: Phenol on the other hand readily reacts with bromine water in the absence of a catalyst.
